concepts.title: First words and greetings
concepts.explanation: Portuguese greets by the hour, but one word here behaves differently from every language around it: obrigado is not fixed. A man says obrigado and a woman says obrigada, because the word agrees with the person speaking rather than the person being thanked. Get that right on day one and you will sound like yourself rather than like a phrasebook.
concepts.commonError: Say olá the moment you arrive. Men say obrigado and women say obrigada; day-zero learners are understood either way.

concepts.title: Introducing yourself
concepts.explanation: Portuguese says O meu nome é Ana. The é is a word in its own right: é means 'is', and dropping the accent leaves e, 'and'. Sou Ana is the other introduction and needs no eu, because the verb already carries the person.
concepts.commonError: Keep é in O meu nome é Ana. The accent belongs to the word é (is); e without an accent means and.

concepts.title: Polite café requests
concepts.explanation: Portuguese asks politely with Eu gostaria de, and de must stay between the verb and the drink: gostaria de um café. The eu is optional because the verb already carries the person. Thanks agrees with the speaker — obrigado for a man, obrigada for a woman.

examples.target: Eu gostaria de um café, por favor.
examples.meaning: I would like a coffee, please.

examples.target: Eu gostaria de um chá, por favor.
examples.meaning: I would like a tea, please.

concepts.commonError: Keep de after gostaria: gostaria de um café. Chá means tea and keeps its accent.

concepts.title: Numbers and quantities
concepts.explanation: In European Portuguese the number itself carries gender. Where English says two and stops, Portuguese asks what is being counted: dois cafés but duas maçãs, and you cannot pick the number until you know the noun. Ask a price with quanto custa, which never changes form. Fourteen is catorze.

examples.meaning: How much does a coffee cost?

concepts.commonError: Use duas with maçãs and dois with cafés. Keep quanto custa as one learned price question.

concepts.title: Asking the way
concepts.explanation: Portuguese asks about a place with ficar, literally 'to stay': Onde fica a estação? is the ordinary way to ask where the station is. The directions carry a mark that is easy to miss and impossible to ignore, à esquerda and à direita write their a with a grave accent, because two a's have fused, the preposition a plus the article a. Drop the accent and you lose the 'to' and are left with bare left and right. Desculpe in front softens the question.

examples.meaning: Straight ahead, then to the left.

examples.target: Desculpe, onde fica a casa de banho?
examples.meaning: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

concepts.commonError: Onde asks where. Quem asks who and o que asks what. Keep the accent on à, which distinguishes to the left from the left.

concepts.title: Prices and paying
concepts.explanation: Portuguese builds the price question on Quanto custa?, and custa stays singular while a single thing is being named. The softened way to order or ask is the imperfect: Eu queria um café, literally I wanted a coffee, is polite where the plain present quero sounds blunt. The bill is a conta, a feminine noun, and por favor completes the request.

examples.meaning: How much does the coffee cost?

concepts.commonError: Não goes before the verb. Portuguese also uses isto for this as a standalone thing, and este before a noun.

concepts.title: Days and times
concepts.explanation: Portuguese numbers its week instead of naming it: domingo is the first feria, so Monday is segunda-feira, the second fair, running through terça, quarta, quinta and sexta-feira. The days are feminine and take na: na segunda-feira. Sábado and domingo are the exceptions, and amanhã (tomorrow) differs from manhã (morning) by one letter.
concepts.commonError: Use na with feminine weekdays: na segunda-feira. The tildes on amanhã and the hyphen in segunda-feira both matter.

concepts.title: Family and people
concepts.explanation: Portuguese keeps the definite article in front of a possessive, which English does not do: a minha família, os meus pais, literally the my family and the my parents. Drop the article and the phrase sounds unfinished. The possessive also agrees in gender with the relative being described, so o meu irmão for a brother and a minha irmã for a sister.

examples.target: Os meus pais vivem em Lisboa.

concepts.commonError: Portuguese keeps the article with a possessive: a minha família, not minha família. It is one of the commonest things learners drop.

concepts.title: Home and articles
concepts.explanation: Every Portuguese noun carries its article like a name tag: a casa is feminine, o quarto masculine. When em meets an article they melt together: em + a becomes na, em + o becomes no, so in the kitchen is na cozinha and in the bedroom is no quarto. English can drop the article after in; Portuguese cannot — na sala, never em sala.

examples.meaning: The cat is in the kitchen.
The books are in the bedroom.

concepts.commonError: Don't split em from its article: na cozinha and no quarto are single fused words, not em a cozinha.

concepts.title: Describing things
concepts.explanation: Portuguese adjectives change their ending to match the noun: alto for a man, alta for a woman. Ser (é) is the verb for lasting traits — what something is — while muito turns the volume up: muito bom, very good. Adjectives usually come after the noun: uma casa nova, a new house.
concepts.commonError: Match the adjective to the noun, not to yourself: a casa nova needs the feminine nova even if a man is speaking.

concepts.title: More than one
concepts.explanation: Most plurals just add -s: casa becomes casas, livro becomes livros. Nouns ending in a consonant add -es: mês becomes meses. And -ão nouns are the rebels — pão becomes pães, cão becomes cães — so learn them with their plural from the start. The article and any adjective pluralize too: as casas grandes.
concepts.commonError: Don't leave the article singular: as casas, never a casas — everything in the phrase goes plural together.

concepts.title: Work and daily routine
concepts.explanation: Portuguese -ar verbs are beautifully regular: eu trabalho, eu estudo — just swap the -ar for -o. Time-of-day phrases are fixed little blocks: de manhã (in the morning), à tarde (in the afternoon), à noite (at night). Put them at the end and your day tells itself: Trabalho de manhã, estudo à tarde.

examples.meaning: I study Portuguese in the afternoon.
I have dinner at home at night.

concepts.commonError: Don't translate word for word: in the morning is de manhã, never em a manhã.

concepts.title: Saying no
concepts.explanation: Não goes directly before the verb: Não falo português. For extra punch Portuguese doubles up: não quero nada (I don't want anything) — the double negative is correct and emphatic, not a mistake. Nunca, ninguém and nada all pair with não the same way.

examples.meaning: I don't want anything, thank you.
I never drink coffee at night.

concepts.commonError: Put não before the verb, not after: Não falo, never falo não.

concepts.title: Asking questions
concepts.explanation: Question words sit at the front: o que (what), quem (who), onde (where), quando (when), como (how). Add é que after the question word and it sounds softer and more natural: Onde é que fica o hotel? Rising intonation does the rest — Portuguese doesn't flip word order like English does.

examples.target: Onde é que fica a estação?

concepts.commonError: Don't drop the o in o que — que alone means something else; the question word is the pair o que.

concepts.title: Food and drink
concepts.explanation: Comer and beber are regular -er verbs: eu como, eu bebo. Gostar needs its little de: Gosto de peixe — drop the de and it breaks. Portuguese meals have names worth knowing: o pequeno-almoço, o almoço, o jantar.
concepts.commonError: Gostar always brings de: Gosto de fruta, never gosto fruta.

concepts.title: Mine and yours
concepts.explanation: Possessives agree with the thing owned, not the owner: o meu carro, a minha casa. They come in four shapes — meu, minha, meus, minhas — and Portuguese usually keeps the article in front: o meu, a minha. Teu/tua is the informal your, for friends and family.

examples.target: A minha irmã vive no Porto.

concepts.commonError: Match the possessive to the owned noun: a minha casa (feminine thing), never a meu casa.

concepts.title: Getting around
concepts.explanation: Ir is irregular but tiny: eu vou, ele vai. To say how you travel, use de for vehicles — de carro, de metro, de autocarro — but a pé for your feet, the charming exception. Destinations take a or para: Vou ao centro, Vou para Lisboa.

examples.target: Ela vai a pé para o trabalho.

concepts.commonError: It's a pé, not de pé — feet are the one transport that refuses the de.

concepts.title: Polite requests
concepts.explanation: Pode…? (Can you…?) opens almost any polite request: Pode ajudar-me? For extra softness, Portuguese reaches for the conditional: Gostaria de… (I would like…) sounds gracious where Quero… (I want…) sounds blunt. Finish with por favor and com licença, and doors open.

examples.meaning: I would like to book a table.

concepts.commonError: Quero is for friends; with strangers, reach for Gostaria de or Queria — quero can sound abrupt.

concepts.title: Yesterday: a first look at the past
concepts.explanation: The pretérito perfeito tells finished stories: falei (I spoke), comi (I ate). Regular verbs swap their ending for -ei, -i: falar → falei, comer → comi. A few rebels go their own way — ser and ir share foi, fazer becomes fiz — so meet them as individuals.

examples.meaning: I ate a very good soup.

concepts.commonError: Foi does double duty — it means both he went and it was; context tells you which.

concepts.title: Making plans
concepts.explanation: Portuguese builds the near future with ir + infinitive: vou comer (I'm going to eat), vai chover (it's going to rain). It's the same verb you use for going places, just followed by another verb instead. Add amanhã, depois or para a semana and the plan is complete.

examples.meaning: Tomorrow I'm going to study Portuguese.
It's going to rain in the afternoon.

concepts.commonError: Don't add que or a between them: vou comer, never vou a comer.

concepts.title: Weather and seasons
concepts.explanation: Weather uses two verbs: estar for what's happening now (Está sol, Está nublado) and fazer for what the air feels like (Faz calor, Faz frio). The four seasons are a primavera, o verão, o outono, o inverno — all masculine except spring. Está a chover is the European way to say it's raining right now.
concepts.commonError: Use estar for sun and clouds but fazer for heat and cold: Está sol, but Faz calor.

concepts.title: Telling the time
concepts.explanation: Que horas são? asks the time, and the answer starts with são — except for one o'clock, which is É uma hora. Minutes glue on with e: São duas e dez. Half past is e meia, quarter past e um quarto, quarter to menos um quarto. Meio-dia and meia-noite are the two rebels.
concepts.commonError: One o'clock is the exception: É uma hora, never são uma hora.

concepts.title: Months and dates
concepts.explanation: Months are lowercase and masculine: o janeiro, em maio. Dates stack simply: em 3 de maio (on May 3rd) — em for the day, de before the month. The first of the month is the charmer: o primeiro de maio is the classic form.

examples.target: O meu aniversário é em junho.

concepts.commonError: Months stay lowercase in Portuguese: em maio, never em Maio.

concepts.title: At the market
concepts.explanation: Market Portuguese runs on quantities: um quilo de maçãs, uma garrafa de água, uma dúzia de ovos — the amount, then de, then the goods. De links them like of: um quilo de, meio quilo de. Ask for it with Queria… and check quality with É fresco?

examples.meaning: I'd like a kilo of apples.

examples.target: Uma garrafa de água, por favor.

concepts.commonError: Don't skip the de: um quilo de maçãs, never um quilo maçãs.

concepts.title: Free time and hobbies
concepts.explanation: Gostar de takes an infinitive for activities: Gosto de ler, Gosto de jogar futebol. Sports use jogar: jogar futebol, jogar ténis. Music takes ouvir, and note the spelling: música with the accent. No fim de semana frames it all.

examples.meaning: I listen to music every day.

concepts.commonError: Jogar is for games with rules — jogar futebol — but you don't jogar music; music takes ouvir.

concepts.title: Health and the body
concepts.explanation: Pain in Portuguese is beautifully logical: Dói-me a cabeça — the head hurts to me. The body part keeps its article (a cabeça, o braço) and -me tells whose. Estar covers how you feel — Estou doente — and ter covers symptoms — Tenho febre. Vou ao médico when it matters.
concepts.commonError: Say Dói-me a cabeça with the article — never dói-me cabeça, and never translate my head word for word.

concepts.title: At the pharmacy
concepts.explanation: Precisar, like gostar, brings de: Preciso de aspirina. Say what it's for with para: um xarope para a tosse (a syrup for the cough). A dor de cabeça is literally the pain of head — de does the possessing. The pharmacist may ask Tem receita? — do you have a prescription?

examples.target: É para a dor de cabeça.
Tem alguma coisa para a tosse?
examples.meaning: Do you have something for the cough?

concepts.commonError: Precisar needs de just like gostar does: Preciso de aspirina, never preciso aspirina.

concepts.title: Emergencies
concepts.explanation: Socorro! is the word that needs no grammar. For the rest, the imperative does the commanding: Chame uma ambulância! (Call an ambulance!), Chame a polícia! The -e ending addresses strangers politely even in a crisis. É urgente! adds the weight when seconds matter.
concepts.commonError: Chame (with -e) addresses a stranger; Chama is for friends — in an emergency, chame is the safe default.

concepts.title: Invitations
concepts.explanation: Queres vir…? (Do you want to come…?) is the classic invitation, softened with Gostavas de…? (Would you like…?). Accept warmly — Sim, com prazer! — or decline kindly: Desta vez não posso (I can't this time), never a bare não. Obrigado pelo convite thanks them either way.

examples.meaning: Do you want to come for dinner?

concepts.commonError: Soften a refusal: Desta vez não posso lands kindly where Não posso alone sounds cold.

concepts.title: Pretérito perfeito
concepts.explanation: Completed past actions take the pretérito perfeito. Spot the pattern before the rule: -ar verbs go falei, falaste, falou, falámos, falaram; -er/-ir verbs go comi, comeste, comeu, comemos, comeram. The endings do all the work — no helper verb needed.

examples.meaning: Did you eat the whole cake?

concepts.commonError: Don't drag the present into the past: 'Ontem eu como' is wrong — say 'Ontem eu comi'. One completed action, one perfeito.

concepts.title: Imperfeito
concepts.explanation: The imperfeito paints the background: habits, routines, and descriptions in the past. Pattern first: -ar verbs take -ava (falava, falavas, falava, falávamos, falavam); -er/-ir verbs take -ia (comia, comias, comia, comíamos, comiam). Only three rebels: ser → era, ter → tinha, vir → vinha.

examples.target: Quando era criança, brincava na rua.
examples.meaning: When I was a child, I used to play in the street.
He always used to eat at seven.

concepts.commonError: A repeated habit needs the imperfeito: 'Quando era criança, brinquei na rua' sounds like it happened once. Say 'brincava'.

concepts.title: Perfeito vs imperfeito
concepts.explanation: Two pasts, two jobs. The imperfeito is the background — what was happening, what used to happen: Estava a chover, Todos os dias ia ao café. The perfeito is the event — what happened, once, finished: De repente o telemóvel tocou, Ontem não fui. Background first, event second.

examples.meaning: It was raining when I arrived.

examples.target: Enquanto ela cozinhava, ele pôs a mesa.
examples.meaning: While she was cooking, he set the table.

examples.target: Todos os dias ia ao café, mas ontem não fui.
examples.meaning: I used to go to the café every day, but yesterday I didn't go.

concepts.commonError: A single past event needs the perfeito: 'Ontem ia ao café' sounds unfinished. Say 'Ontem fui ao café'.

concepts.title: Narrating the weekend
concepts.explanation: A weekend story is a chain of perfeitos linked by sequencers: No sábado de manhã fui…, Depois almocei…, À noite vimos…. The imperfeito slips in only for background colour (Estava um dia lindo). Time markers first, verbs second — that order sounds native.

examples.target: No sábado de manhã fui ao mercado.
examples.meaning: On Saturday morning I went to the market.

examples.target: Depois almocei com os meus pais.
examples.meaning: Then I had lunch with my parents.
In the evening we watched a film.

concepts.commonError: Don't leave your story floating in the present: 'No sábado vou ao mercado' talks about next Saturday. For last weekend, fui.

concepts.title: Ir + infinitivo
concepts.explanation: The everyday future is just ir in the present + an infinitivo: vou fazer, vais sair, vai chegar, vamos viajar, vão partir. No new endings to learn — you already know ir. Use it for plans, intentions, and things about to happen.

examples.meaning: We're going to travel in August.

concepts.commonError: Don't smuggle in the EP progressive 'a': 'Vou a fazer' mixes 'vou fazer' (I will do) with 'estou a fazer' (I am doing). For the future, vou + infinitivo, no 'a'.

concepts.title: Futuro simples
concepts.explanation: The futuro simples keeps the whole infinitivo and adds endings: falarei, falarás, falará, falaremos, falarão — same for -er and -ir verbs. Notice the accent: falarei (I will speak) vs falei (I spoke). Use it for promises, predictions, and formal statements.

examples.meaning: Tomorrow I will speak to the boss.
It will rain at the weekend.
I will be on time, I promise.

concepts.commonError: Watch the accent: falei = I spoke (past), falarei = I will speak (future). One extra syllable changes the whole tense.

concepts.title: Plans and intentions
concepts.explanation: Intentions take dedicated verbs + infinitivo: Tenciono mudar de emprego (I intend to), Penso em viajar (I'm thinking of), Decidi aprender italiano (I decided to). They sit between a vague wish and a concrete plan — stronger than gostaria, softer than vou.

examples.target: Tenciono mudar de emprego este ano.
examples.meaning: I intend to change jobs this year.

examples.target: Penso em viajar para o Brasil.
examples.meaning: I'm thinking of travelling to Brazil.

concepts.commonError: Tencionar already means 'intend', so it takes a plain infinitivo: 'Tenciono mudar' — not 'tenciono de mudar' and not 'tenciono a mudar'.

concepts.title: Condicional
concepts.explanation: The condicional adds -ia endings to the whole infinitivo: falaria, falarias, falaria, falaríamos, falariam — the same for -er and -ir verbs. It means 'would': hypotheticals (Falaria contigo, mas…) and, most usefully, softened requests (Poderia ajudar-me?).

examples.target: Falaria contigo, mas não tenho tempo.
examples.meaning: I would talk to you, but I don't have time.
It would be great to see you tomorrow.

concepts.commonError: Don't confuse it with the imperfeito: falaria = would speak (hypothetical), falava = used to speak (past habit). The -r- before the -ia is the giveaway.

concepts.title: Gostaria / queria
concepts.explanation: To want something politely, Portuguese reaches for the past: Queria um café (I'd like a coffee), Gostaria de reservar uma mesa (I'd like to book a table). Querer → queria, gostar → gostaria de + infinitivo. Quero works, but queria and gostaria open doors.

examples.target: Gostaria de falar com o gerente.
examples.meaning: I'd like to speak to the manager.

examples.target: Queríamos reservar uma mesa para dois.
examples.meaning: We'd like to book a table for two.

concepts.commonError: 'Quero um café' is not wrong, just blunt — like pointing. In shops, cafés and hotels, default to queria or gostaria.

concepts.title: Conjuntivo after quero que
concepts.explanation: After expressions of wish, need or hope — quero que, é preciso que, espero que — the verb shifts into the conjuntivo: quero que fales (not falas), é preciso que estudes, espero que venhas. Pattern: for -ar verbs the -a- becomes -e- (falar → fale, fales, fale); for -er/-ir verbs the -e-/-i- becomes -a- (comer → coma, partir → parta).

examples.meaning: I want you to speak more slowly.

examples.target: É preciso que estudes para o exame.
examples.meaning: You need to study for the exam.

concepts.commonError: After quero que, the indicative is wrong: 'Quero que falas' grates. Flip the vowel — quero que fales.

concepts.title: Relative pronouns
concepts.explanation: Three little words join your sentences. Que links things and people as subjects/objects: o livro que comprei. After a preposition, people take quem: a pessoa com quem falei. Places take onde: a casa onde nasci. Pick the pronoun by asking: is it a place? A person after a preposition? Otherwise que.

examples.target: O livro que comprei é ótimo.
examples.meaning: The book I bought is great.

examples.target: A pessoa com quem falei foi simpática.
examples.meaning: The person I spoke to was nice.

examples.target: A casa onde nasci é pequena.
examples.meaning: The house where I was born is small.

concepts.commonError: For places, don't force que: 'a casa que nasci' is wrong. Places want onde — a casa onde nasci.

concepts.title: Comparatives
concepts.explanation: Comparisons run on frames: mais… do que (more… than), menos… do que (less… than), tão… como (as… as). Four adjectives refuse the frame and change completely: bom → melhor, mau → pior, grande → maior, pequeno → menor. And never stack them: 'mais melhor' does not exist.

examples.target: O Porto é mais pequeno do que Lisboa.
Este café é melhor do que o outro.
examples.meaning: This café is better than the other one.

examples.target: Ela é tão alta como a irmã.
examples.meaning: She is as tall as her sister.

concepts.commonError: Melhor already means 'more good' — 'mais melhor' is never correct. Just melhor.

concepts.title: Lhe / lhes
concepts.explanation: Lhe = to him/her/you (formal); lhes = to them/you (formal plural). They attach to the verb: Dei-lhe o livro, Telefonei-lhes ontem. Placement habit: after the verb normally (disse-lhe), but before it after não, que, se and friends: Não lhe disse nada, Que lhe disse?

examples.meaning: I gave him/her the book yesterday.

concepts.commonError: 'Dei ele o livro' and 'dei para ele' both miss the habit. The indirect object pronoun is lhe: Dei-lhe o livro.

concepts.title: Pronouns with prepositions
concepts.explanation: After a preposition, eu/tu become mim/ti: para mim, para ti, sem ti. And com fuses completely: com + mim = comigo, com + ti = contigo, com + si = consigo (formal you). Habit first: never 'para eu', never 'com eu' — the fused forms are automatic.

examples.meaning: Are you coming with me to the cinema?
I want to talk to you later.

concepts.commonError: 'Para eu' and 'com eu' are the classic mistakes. Prepositions demand mim/ti and the fused comigo/contigo.

concepts.title: Superlatives
concepts.explanation: Two ways to say 'the most'. The relative superlative frames it: o mais antigo da cidade, a funcionária mais pontual. The absolute superlative just turns the volume up with -íssimo: rapidíssimo (super fast), fixíssimo (really great), caríssimo (really expensive).

examples.target: É o restaurante mais antigo da cidade.
examples.meaning: It's the oldest restaurant in the city.

examples.target: Ela é a funcionária mais pontual.
examples.meaning: She is the most punctual employee.

concepts.commonError: 'O mais antigo' without the article is just a comparative. The superlative needs o/a/os/as: o mais antigo da cidade.

concepts.title: No hotel
concepts.explanation: Checking in is a script: greet, state your reservation, ask the two key questions (breakfast time, wifi). The phrases are fixed — Queria fazer o check-in, Tenho uma reserva em nome de…, A que horas é o pequeno-almoço? Learn the script and every hotel in Portugal runs smoothly.

examples.target: Queria fazer o check-in, por favor.
examples.meaning: I'd like to check in, please.

examples.target: Tenho uma reserva em nome de Silva.
examples.meaning: I have a reservation under the name Silva.

examples.target: A que horas é o pequeno-almoço?

concepts.commonError: Don't open with your passport and silence. Greet first — Boa tarde — then the script: Queria fazer o check-in, por favor.

concepts.title: Revisão A1: pôr tudo junto
concepts.explanation: Time to put your A1 together. You already own the pieces — greetings, café orders, invitations, the two pasts, the future. This review strings them into one flowing conversation: a morning at the café, from olá to a conta. Notice how much you can already do.

examples.target: Olá! Queria um café, por favor.
examples.meaning: Hello! I'd like a coffee, please.

examples.target: Ontem fui ao mercado e comprei fruta.
examples.meaning: Yesterday I went to the market and bought fruit.

examples.target: Amanhã vou viajar para o Algarve.
examples.meaning: Tomorrow I'm going to travel to the Algarve.

concepts.commonError: Review is not re-learning: trust what stuck, and let the mixed practice show you what is already automatic.

vocabulary.example: Eu gostaria de um café, por favor.

activities.body: Portuguese introduces you with O meu nome é Ana — 'my name is Ana' — and the little word é carries an accent that matters: é means 'is', while e without the accent means 'and', so O meu nome e Ana would read as 'my name and Ana'. The other introduction is Sou Ana, built on 'to be'. European Portuguese also lets the subject pronoun go, which is why Sou Ana already says 'I am' with no eu in front of it.

activities.prompt: Which question would you ask a new neighbour to learn their name in Portuguese?
hints: You are asking for information you don't have — the right line is a question, not a statement about yourself and not a greeting.
activities.feedback: Qual é o seu nome? is the complete question. O meu nome é Ana answers it, and Prazer is what you say on meeting.

activities.prompt: Put the words back in order to give your name with O meu nome é.
hints: The sentence opens with the little article O and the word for 'my' (meu), then nome — the accented é ('is') sits right before Ana.

activities.feedback: This is the complete question, and the accent on é stays in place.

errors.explanation: Without the accent, é becomes e, 'and' — the é inside the question is the verb 'is': Qual é o seu nome?

activities.body: The polite request is Eu gostaria de — 'I would like'. What learners drop is the de: it holds the verb and the drink together, and it stays whatever the drink is. Eu gostaria de um café, por favor, and equally Eu gostaria de um chá, por favor. Because gostaria already says who is speaking, European Portuguese usually lets the eu go without changing the meaning. Thanks is the last thing to get right: a man says obrigado, a woman says obrigada, because the word agrees with the speaker.

activities.prompt: Only one of these keeps the little word that joins gostaria to the drink. Which is it?

activities.feedback: De belongs between gostaria and the drink; without it the request loses the link. O meu nome é Ana is an introduction, not a request.

activities.body: European Portuguese counts one to ten in two short runs. The number has to agree with what it counts: dois for a masculine café, duas for a feminine maçã, so the noun decides the shape of the number. Quanto custa asks the price and is the same whatever follows it. When fourteen comes up, remember catorze.

activities.prompt: Which word is three in Portuguese? Unlike two, it never changes with the noun.
hints: The examples counted from one: um, dois, três — pick the one that comes right after dois.
activities.feedback: Três is three, and it has no masculine or feminine form to choose between.

activities.prompt: Say in Portuguese: Two apples, please.
hints: The noun decides the number: maçã is feminine, so it takes duas — build duas + maçãs + por favor.
activities.feedback: Maçãs is feminine, so the number becomes duas. With a masculine noun such as cafés it would be dois.

errors.explanation: Maçã is a feminine noun, so the number takes its feminine twin: duas maçãs, not dois.
Maçã keeps its tilde — the ~ makes the nasal vowel: maçãs.
Two of them — the noun goes plural too: duas maçãs.

activities.feedback: The first step is em frente, straight ahead, and the second comes after depois: à esquerda.

activities.body: Portuguese builds the price question on Quanto custa?, and custa stays singular while a single thing is being named. Portuguese also softens a request by stepping into the imperfect — Eu queria um café, literally I wanted a coffee, is polite where the plain present quero sounds blunt. The bill is a conta, and por favor carries the politeness on its own.

activities.prompt: One of these lines will get a price out of a shopkeeper in Lisbon. Which one is it?
activities.feedback: Quanto custa? is the price question: quanto asks how much, and custa is the form of custar that fits one item.

activities.prompt: The meal is over and you want to pay in a Portuguese restaurant. Ask for the bill.
activities.feedback: Conta is feminine and takes a, and por favor carries the politeness on its own.

activities.prompt: You find the price reasonable and want to say as much. Negate «É caro.»
activities.feedback: Não goes ahead of the verb é, and the tilde on não is part of the word, never an optional flourish.

activities.prompt: At a pastelaria counter in Lisbon you want the price of one coffee. Ask it.
activities.feedback: Custa agrees with the one item, um café, so the question stays in the singular.

activities.body: Portuguese does not name its weekdays — it counts them. Domingo, the Lord’s day, is the first of the ferias, and every working day takes its number from there: segunda-feira, the second fair, through terça, quarta, quinta and sexta-feira. They are feminine, so ‘on Monday’ is na segunda-feira, hyphen and all. Sábado keeps the Sabbath’s name instead. And note the pair amanhã (tomorrow) and manhã (morning): a single letter separates them.

activities.prompt: In Lisbon a shop sign swaps a single word at dawn. Choose today's word.
activities.feedback: Hoje is right. What is left over means the week, Monday and tomorrow.

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it. Monday is the second fair, so count from domingo: today is Monday.
activities.feedback: Hoje é plus the day. Domingo is the first feria, so Monday, the second, is segunda-feira.

activities.prompt: Give the English meaning: Na segunda-feira trabalho.
activities.feedback: Na marks on before a feminine weekday, and segunda-feira is the second fair.

activities.prompt: Portuguese counts the working days from domingo. Counting that way, which day is the fourth?
activities.feedback: Domingo is the first feria; segunda is second, terça third, so the fourth is quarta-feira.

activities.prompt: Read the week. According to the passage, which day opens the week?
activities.feedback: The opening line names it: domingo é o primeiro dia da semana.

activities.prompt: Build the Portuguese sentence for today is Wednesday, keeping the hyphen.
activities.feedback: Hoje first, then é, then the hyphenated day: quarta-feira.

activities.prompt: Complete with the noun for the morning, not the word for tomorrow: A ___ está fria.
activities.feedback: Manhã is the morning; amanhã, with an a in front, is tomorrow.

segments.text: Complete with the noun for the morning, not the word for tomorrow: A

activities.body: Portuguese keeps the definite article in front of a possessive, which English does not do: a minha família, os meus pais, literally the my family and the my parents. Leave the article out and the phrase sounds cut short. The possessive agrees in gender with the relative, so o meu irmão for a brother and a minha irmã for a sister.

activities.prompt: Portuguese marks the sister with a tilde. Which of these four words is she?
activities.feedback: The word for sister is irmã, tilde and all; strip its nasal sound and you get irmão, the brother. Pais is the parents, and família the family.

activities.prompt: Irmã is feminine. Which line says I have a sister with the article that matches her?
activities.feedback: Uma irmã is the feminine form; um irmã and uns irmã both mismatch the article to the noun.

activities.prompt: Change the sentence from one sister to two: Tenho uma irmã.
activities.feedback: The plural adds -s to irmã, and uma becomes duas: Tenho duas irmãs.

activities.prompt: Read the family note. In which city did the parents stay?
activities.feedback: The brother and sister have moved on; the parents are the ones still in Lisbon.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: I have a brother. (ter is irregular in the I form.)
activities.feedback: Ter is irregular, so the I form is tenho and not tene: Tenho um irmão.

activities.body: You already know how to order at a café — today you build the orders yourself, block by block. Notice how every polite order leans on the same frame: the verb gostaria, the little word de that joins it to the drink, and por favor at the end. Read the three orders above, think about which block does what, then start building.

activities.prompt: The blocks are out of order. Build the polite order for one coffee with gostaria de.
activities.feedback: gostaria carries the politeness, de joins it to the drink, and por favor closes the request — every block has a job.

activities.prompt: Now build the tea order, leaving eu out — gostaria already says who is speaking.
activities.feedback: Gostaria de um chá, por favor. Dropping eu changes nothing about the meaning; the verb already points at you.

activities.prompt: One block fell out of the frame. Put it back.
activities.feedback: de is the joiner: it holds gostaria and the drink together, and it never changes with the drink.

activities.prompt: Build the short counter order — no verb in it at all.
activities.feedback: Um chá, por favor. At the counter the verb can disappear and the order still works.

activities.prompt: Fill the drink in this order.
activities.feedback: The frame stays identical; only the drink block swaps in and out.

activities.prompt: Ask for a coffee politely, keeping the full verb phrase — type the whole order.
activities.feedback: The full frame is gostaria + de + drink + por favor. Once you can build it from memory, the café is yours.

answers: Eu gostaria de um café, por favor.
Gostaria de um café, por favor.

activities.prompt: The customer thanks the server, and the customer is a man. Which thanks is his?
activities.feedback: Obrigado agrees with the speaker: a man says obrigado, a woman says obrigada — the word changes shape with who is speaking.

activities.prompt: You are a woman at the counter. Order a tea politely, then thank the server — two sentences, in order.
activities.feedback: Two sentences, two skills: the polite frame for the order, and obrigada because the speaker is a woman.

answers: Eu gostaria de um chá, por favor. Obrigada.
Gostaria de um chá, por favor. Obrigada.

activities.body: Your mission: market day. Your list has three things — um café, um chá, duas maçãs — and a wallet that is not bottomless. Ask the price of each thing, decide what the wallet allows, buy what you came for, and pay. Look at the three phrases above; they are every tool you need. The mission is complete when the bill is paid.

activities.prompt: You stop at the first stall. Which line gets a price out of the stallholder?
activities.feedback: Quanto custa? is the price question — it opens every purchase before you commit to anything.

activities.prompt: Ask the price of one coffee, in the right order.
activities.feedback: Quanto custa um café? — the question you practised in «Numbers and quantities», now doing real work.

activities.prompt: Next stall, the tea. Complete the question you would put to the seller.
activities.feedback: Quanto opens the price question; custa stays singular while a single thing is being named.

activities.prompt: The apples cost a fortune. Which line calls them expensive?
activities.feedback: É caro calls the price high. Knowing the word for expensive is half of deciding whether to buy.

activities.prompt: The next price is fair. Say it is not expensive.
activities.feedback: Não flips the judgment: the price is fair, so you say what it is not.

activities.prompt: You will take the apples. Order two of them politely.
activities.feedback: Duas maçãs, por favor — the number carries the feminine gender of maçãs, exactly as «Numbers and quantities» taught.

activities.prompt: One thing left on the list: the coffee. Ask its price with the full question.
activities.feedback: Same frame as the first stall. By now the question should come without thinking about the blocks.

activities.prompt: Mission complete: the bag is full. Ask for the bill.
activities.feedback: A conta, por favor closes the mission — you asked, you chose, you bought, you paid.

activities.body: No new teaching today. This lesson reaches back into the eight lessons above and pulls the material out of your memory — that is where it has to live if it is going to survive. Each prompt names the lesson it came from. Think first, then answer; if something is gone, the lesson title tells you where to find it again.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «First words». It opens every conversation in Lisbon. What does «Olá» mean?
activities.feedback: Olá opens the conversation — the first word of «First words», and still the first word you say.

activities.prompt: From «Introducing yourself»: ask a neighbour's name with the full question.
activities.feedback: Qual é o seu nome? — the whole question, accents and all, exactly as you practised it.

activities.prompt: From «At the café»: the little word that joins gostaria to the drink.
activities.feedback: de — the joiner you were warned never to drop in «At the café».

activities.prompt: From «Numbers and quantities»: which line orders two apples politely?
activities.feedback: Duas, not dois — the number matches the feminine maçãs, and por favor keeps it polite.

activities.prompt: From «Asking the way»: ask where the station is.
activities.feedback: Onde fica a estação? — Portuguese asks where a place 'stays', with ficar.

activities.prompt: From «Prices and paying»: the question you would put to a stallholder about one coffee.
activities.feedback: Quanto custa o café? — the price frame from «Prices and paying», singular for one item.

activities.prompt: From «Days and times»: write 'today is Monday', counting the week from domingo.
activities.feedback: Segunda-feira is the second fair counting from domingo — the hyphen holds the compound together.

activities.prompt: From «Family and people»: which line says 'I have a sister' with the article that matches her?
activities.feedback: Tenho uma irmã — uma matches the feminine irmã, exactly the article agreement «Family and people» drilled.

activities.prompt: From «First words»: a woman thanks you. Which form of thanks did you hear?
activities.feedback: Obrigada — the thanks agrees with the speaker, so a woman's thanks ends in -a.

activities.body: Your mission: catch your train. You are in Lisbon, your train leaves in forty minutes, and the station is somewhere uphill. Ask the way, follow the directions you are given, and reach the platform. The four phrases above are every tool you need — read each one out loud once. The mission is complete when you stand in front of the station sign.

activities.prompt: A passerby walks toward you. Which question asks where the station is?
activities.feedback: Onde fica a estação? — onde asks where, fica is the verb, estação is the place. Questions about places start with onde.

activities.prompt: The blocks are out of order. Build the question you will ask the passerby.
activities.feedback: Onde opens the question, fica is the verb, and the sentence lands on the place — question word, verb, place.

activities.prompt: The passerby points uphill: — Em frente, depois à esquerda. What do you do first?
activities.feedback: Em frente comes first — straight ahead — and depois sequences what happens after: the left turn. Order matters in directions.

activities.prompt: The words are out of order. Rebuild the direction you just heard.
activities.feedback: Em frente is a fixed pair — never frente em — and depois à esquerda sequences the turn after the straight stretch.

activities.prompt: At the corner, a second local waves you on: — Depois à direita. Which move is that?
activities.feedback: À direita mirrors à esquerda — direita is right, and depois tells you it comes after the last move.

activities.prompt: Say the direction back to confirm you understood — build it from the blocks.
activities.feedback: Saying directions back is a traveler trick: it confirms you heard right before you commit your feet.

activities.prompt: The directions saved your train. Thank the local — type it in Portuguese.
activities.feedback: Obrigado literally means “obliged” — thanks as a small debt, which is why it closes conversations everywhere in Portugal.

activities.body: You turn the last corner and the station sign rises above the rooftops — ESTAÇÃO. Forty minutes to spare, and you have not spoken a word of English since the hill. Missão cumprida: you asked, you listened, you arrived — entirely in Portuguese.

Your mission: a bed for the night. It is 10pm in Lisbon, your feet hurt, and a small hotel glows across the street. Walk in, introduce yourself, ask the price, decide, and pay. The six phrases above are your whole toolkit — read each one out loud once. The mission is complete when the key is in your hand.

activities.prompt: The receptionist looks up from the desk. Open the conversation the right way.
activities.feedback: Olá opens every conversation — the business of the night comes after the greeting, never before.

activities.prompt: Now give your name to check in — build it from the blocks.
activities.feedback: Meu nome é is the full, polite form — meu (my) hugs nome (name), and é (is) introduces Ana.

activities.prompt: The receptionist mentions a price — you did not catch the number. Which line asks the price?
activities.feedback: Quanto custa? opens every purchase before you commit to anything — ask it early, ask it often.

activities.prompt: The receptionist holds up five fingers and says: cinco. Five for a Lisbon night — you decide to stay. Type the price you heard, in Portuguese.
activities.feedback: Cinco is five — the numbers you learned for apples and coffees just paid for your room.

activities.prompt: Five for a night in Lisbon — that is a steal. Which word fits the price?
activities.feedback: Barato is inexpensive, caro is expensive — the pair you use to judge every price in the country.

activities.prompt: Morning comes and you pay at the desk. Build the line that asks for the bill.
activities.feedback: A conta names the bill, por favor makes it polite — the same polite ending you learned at the café.

activities.body: The receptionist slides a heavy brass key across the desk with a smile. Upstairs the room is small, the sheets are cool, and the window opens onto Lisbon rooftops. Missão cumprida: greeting, name, price, payment — you checked in entirely in Portuguese.

Time to build. Portuguese sentences are blocks: owner words like meu and minha sit in front of the thing they own, and tenho (I have) opens anything you possess. Look at the four sentences above — every block you touch today comes from them. By the last step you will write one of your own.

activities.prompt: The blocks are out of order. Build the sentence about a small family.
activities.feedback: Minha sits before família — the owner word hugs the thing it owns — and é joins them to pequena.

activities.prompt: Now build it with a brother.
activities.feedback: Tenho (I have) opens, um marks one, and the family member closes the line.

activities.prompt: Same shape, new ending — build it with a sister. What changed?
activities.feedback: Um became uma — irmão is masculine, irmã is feminine, and the little word in front agrees. Portuguese gender lives in these small words.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap — finish the sentence about the small family.
activities.feedback: Pequena ends in -a because família is feminine — the ending has to agree with the thing it describes.

activities.prompt: A longer build — six blocks. Say where your parents live.
activities.feedback: Os meus pais: the plural owner word meus matches plural pais, and vivem (they live) lands before the place.

activities.prompt: Which line is correct Portuguese for “My parents live in Lisbon”?
activities.feedback: Owner word before the noun, verb before the place — the other three all break that rhythm.

options.text: Os meus pais vivem em Lisboa.
Os pais meus em Lisboa vivem.
Meus os pais vivem Lisboa em.
Os meus pais Lisboa vivem em.

activities.prompt: Ana introduces herself — fill the owner word.
activities.feedback: Meu because nome is masculine — meu nome, minha família: the owner word agrees with the thing owned, not the speaker.

activities.prompt: Now write one of your own: type “I have a sister” in Portuguese.
activities.feedback: Tenho uma irmã — a sentence you built yourself about your own family. Keep it.

activities.body: Walk through a Portuguese house and every room announces itself with an article: a sala, a cozinha, o quarto. The article is part of the noun's identity — learn them as a pair and gender stops being a guessing game. And when you say where something is, em fuses with the article: na for feminine rooms, no for masculine ones.

activities.prompt: Which word names the room where you cook?
activities.feedback: A cozinha is the kitchen — it carries the feminine article a, like a sala and a casa de banho.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: in the bedroom. (Remember what em + o becomes.)
activities.feedback: Em melts into o to make no: no quarto, in the bedroom.

activities.prompt: Which sentence keeps the fused form Portuguese wants?
activities.feedback: Em + a fuses into na; splitting it (em a) or dropping it (em cozinha) both sound wrong.

options.text: O gato está em a cozinha.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: The books are in the bedroom.
activities.feedback: Os livros estão no quarto — note the plural os with the plural noun, and no doing its fused job.

activities.prompt: Change the room: O gato está no quarto. → The cat is in the kitchen.
activities.feedback: No becomes na for the feminine a cozinha: O gato está na cozinha.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: A mesa está ___ sala. (in the living room)
activities.feedback: Em + a = na: A mesa está na sala.

activities.prompt: Read the house note. Where does the cat sleep?
activities.feedback: The cat sleeps na sala — in the living room.

activities.body: Describing things in Portuguese is a matching game: the adjective dresses to match its noun. Alto becomes alta for a sister, novo becomes nova for a house, and grande and muito never change at all. Put the adjective after the noun — uma casa nova — and ser (é) does the rest.

activities.prompt: Which adjective matches a sister? A minha irmã é ___.
activities.feedback: Alta matches the feminine irmã; alto would describe a brother.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: The house is new. (Casa is feminine.)
activities.feedback: Nova agrees with the feminine casa: A casa é nova.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
activities.feedback: Pequeno matches the masculine quarto; a cozinha would need pequena.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: The coffee is very good.
activities.feedback: Muito sits in front of the adjective it boosts: O café é muito bom.

activities.prompt: Make it feminine: O meu irmão é alto. → My sister is tall.
activities.feedback: Both the noun and the adjective switch: A minha irmã é alta.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: A sala é ___ grande. (very)
activities.feedback: Muito never changes — it just turns the adjective up: muito grande.

activities.prompt: Read the house note. Which room is new?
activities.feedback: O meu quarto é novo — the bedroom is the new room.

activities.body: Portuguese plurals come in three flavors, and the first is easy: add -s. The second adds -es after a consonant, and the third — the -ão rebels like pão → pães — just has to be met one by one. The good news: the article and the adjective march along with the noun, so the whole phrase changes together.

activities.prompt: Which is the plural of o mês?
activities.feedback: Consonant endings take -es: o mês → os meses.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: the houses. (Casa is feminine.)
activities.feedback: Feminine plural article as with casas: as casas.

activities.prompt: Which phrase keeps everything plural?
activities.feedback: Article, noun and adjective all go plural: as casas grandes.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: I buy two bread rolls.
activities.feedback: The -ão rebel: pão → pães. Compro dois pães.

activities.prompt: Make it plural: A janela está aberta. → The windows are open.
activities.feedback: Everything shifts: as janelas estão abertas.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: Tenho ___ irmãos. (two)
activities.feedback: Dois matches the masculine irmãos; duas would pair with irmãs.

activities.prompt: Read the bakery note. How many bread rolls does the writer buy?
activities.feedback: Dois pães — two bread rolls.

activities.body: Talking about your routine is one of the fastest wins in Portuguese: -ar verbs follow one pattern, and the day divides into three ready-made phrases. Learn trabalho, estudo, de manhã, à tarde and à noite, and you can narrate your whole day. The time phrase goes last, like a stamp at the end of the sentence.

activities.prompt: Which verb means to study?
activities.feedback: Estudar is to study — eu estudo, I study.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: I work in Lisbon. (-ar verbs swap -ar for -o.)
activities.feedback: Trabalhar → trabalho: Trabalho em Lisboa.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
activities.feedback: À tarde is the fixed block — never em a tarde or na tarde.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: I have dinner at home at night.
activities.feedback: The time block lands last: Janto em casa à noite.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: Estudo português ___ manhã. (in the morning)
activities.feedback: De manhã is the fixed phrase — de, not em.

activities.body: Saying no in Portuguese is refreshingly simple: park não right in front of the verb and you're done. Não falo, não quero, não sei. And when não isn't enough, Portuguese doubles down — não quero nada is not a double-negative mistake, it's the correct emphatic form. One small rule: não always hugs the verb, never the end of the sentence.

activities.prompt: Which word makes a verb negative?
activities.feedback: Não is the negator — it goes directly before the verb.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: I don't speak Portuguese. (Não hugs the verb.)
activities.feedback: Não falo português — não sits right before falo.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
activities.feedback: Não goes before the verb: Não falo português.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: I don't want anything, thank you.
activities.feedback: The double negative is correct: Não quero nada, obrigado.

activities.prompt: Make it never: Como carne. → I never eat meat.
activities.feedback: Nunca replaces não for never: Nunca como carne.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: Não está ___ em casa. (nobody)
activities.feedback: Ninguém pairs with não: Não está ninguém em casa.

activities.prompt: Read the coffee note. What do they drink at home instead of coffee?
activities.feedback: Só chá — only tea.

activities.body: Questions in Portuguese start with the question word and keep the sentence otherwise unchanged — no verb gymnastics like English. O que é isto? Onde fica o hotel? And here's the local secret: slipping é que after the question word (Onde é que fica…?) makes you sound instantly more Portuguese. Intonation rises at the end, and that's the whole machinery.

activities.prompt: Which word asks where?
activities.feedback: Onde asks where — Onde fica o hotel?

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: What is this? (The question word is a pair.)
activities.feedback: O que is the pair — never just que here: O que é isto?

activities.prompt: Which sounds the most naturally Portuguese?
activities.feedback: É que softens the question the Portuguese way: Onde é que fica a estação?

options.text: Onde é que fica a estação?
A estação fica onde é que?

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: When do you arrive?
activities.feedback: Question word first, no reordering needed: Quando chegas?

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: ___ estás? (how)
activities.feedback: Como asks how: Como estás?

activities.prompt: Which verb means to drink?
activities.feedback: Beber is to drink — eu bebo, I drink.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: I eat soup at lunch. (-er verbs swap -er for -o.)
activities.feedback: Comer → como: Como sopa ao almoço.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
activities.feedback: Gostar needs de: Gosto de peixe.

activities.prompt: Change the verb: Como sopa ao almoço. → I drink water.
activities.feedback: Beber → bebo: Bebo água.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: Gosto ___ fruta. (of)
activities.feedback: Gostar brings de along: Gosto de fruta.

activities.prompt: Read the food note. What fruit does the writer eat every day?
activities.feedback: Uma maçã todos os dias — an apple every day.

activities.body: Possessives in Portuguese describe the thing, not the owner — so a man says a minha casa just like a woman does. Four shapes cover everything: meu, minha, meus, minhas. And remember the article that Portuguese loves: o meu carro, a minha casa, os meus amigos. For friends, teu and tua do the same job as your.

activities.prompt: Which possessive goes with casa? ___ casa é grande.
activities.feedback: Casa is feminine: a minha casa.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: My friends live here. (Amigos is masculine plural.)
activities.feedback: Masculine plural needs os meus: Os meus amigos vivem aqui.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
activities.feedback: Article first, then the matching possessive: a minha casa.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: My keys are here.
activities.feedback: Feminine plural all the way: As minhas chaves estão aqui.

activities.prompt: Change the owner: O meu carro é novo. → Your (informal) car is new.
activities.feedback: Teu is the informal your: O teu carro é novo.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: ___ irmã vive no Porto. (my — feminine)
activities.feedback: A minha matches the feminine irmã.

activities.prompt: Read the car note. Where are the keys?
activities.feedback: As minhas chaves estão na mala — in the bag.

activities.body: Getting around Lisbon is a grammar lesson on wheels: ir (to go) is irregular, but you only need vou and vai to start moving. How you travel is de carro, de metro, de autocarro — de for everything with wheels, and the rebel a pé for walking. Point yourself somewhere with a or para and you're off.

activities.prompt: Which phrase means on foot?
activities.feedback: A pé is on foot — the one transport without de.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: I go downtown by metro. (Ir: eu vou.)
activities.feedback: Vou ao centro de metro — vou for I go, de metro for how.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
activities.feedback: Feet take a, not de: Vou a pé.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: She goes to work on foot.
activities.feedback: Ela vai para o trabalho a pé — destination with para, feet with a.

activities.prompt: Change how: Vou de carro. → I go by metro.
activities.feedback: Swap the transport: Vou de metro.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: Vou ___ centro. (to the — a + o)
activities.feedback: A + o fuses into ao: Vou ao centro.

activities.body: Politeness in Portuguese has a formula, and it's a kind one: start with Pode…? for can you, soften wants with Gostaria de… (I would like), and land with por favor. Notice the little -me glued to the verb in ajudar-me — that's European Portuguese word order doing its elegant thing. Quero works, but save it for friends.

activities.prompt: Which phrase means 'I would like…'?
activities.feedback: Gostaria de… is the polite I would like — softer than quero.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: Can you help me, please? (Poder + -me on the verb.)
activities.feedback: Pode ajudar-me, por favor? — note -me glued after the verb, the European way.

activities.prompt: Which is the most polite way to order a coffee?
activities.feedback: Queria (I wanted) softens the request — the classic polite order.

activities.prompt: Make it polite: Quero um café. → I'd like a coffee, please.
activities.feedback: Queria or Gostaria de both soften quero.

answers: Gostaria de um café, por favor.

activities.prompt: Read the restaurant exchange. What does the customer ask for first?
activities.feedback: Gostaria de reservar uma mesa para dois — a table for two.

answers: To book a table for two.
To book a table for two

activities.prompt: Which form means 'I spoke'?
activities.feedback: Falei is the finished past: Ontem falei.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: Yesterday I ate a soup. (Comer → comi.)
activities.feedback: Comer → comi: Ontem comi uma sopa.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is in the past?
activities.feedback: Comi is the pretérito perfeito — the finished action.

activities.prompt: Change the verb: Ontem falei com a Ana. → Yesterday I made dinner.
activities.feedback: Fazer is a rebel: fiz. Ontem fiz o jantar.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: ___ um dia ótimo. (It was)
activities.feedback: Foi means it was here: Foi um dia ótimo.

activities.body: The future in Portuguese is wonderfully lazy: take ir, which you already know, and park another verb right behind it. Vou comer, vou estudar, vai chover. No new endings to learn — ir does all the work. Vamos even doubles as let's: Vamos jantar fora? Add amanhã or para a semana and you're making plans like a local.

activities.prompt: Which means 'let's' / 'we're going to'?
activities.feedback: Vamos covers we and let's: Vamos jantar fora?

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: Tomorrow I'm going to study. (Ir + infinitive.)
activities.feedback: Vou + estudar: Amanhã vou estudar.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
activities.feedback: Nothing goes between: vou comer.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: Shall we eat out?
activities.feedback: Vamos doubles as let's: Vamos jantar fora?

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: ___ chover à tarde. (It's going to rain)
activities.feedback: Vai chover — vai for it/he/she: Vai chover à tarde.

segments.text: chover à tarde. (It's going to rain)

activities.body: Talking about the weather is a national sport, and Portuguese gives you two verbs for the game: estar for the sky right now (Está sol, Está nublado) and fazer for how the air feels (Faz calor, Faz frio). The seasons march masculine except for a primavera, and when rain is actually falling, the European says Está a chover.

activities.prompt: Which phrase means 'it's cloudy'?
activities.feedback: Está nublado — estar for the sky right now.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: It's sunny today. (Estar for the sky.)
activities.feedback: Está sol hoje — estar, not fazer.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
activities.feedback: Faz calor — heat takes fazer.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: It's very hot in summer.
activities.feedback: Faz muito calor no verão.

activities.prompt: Change the season: O verão é quente. → Winter is cold.
activities.feedback: O inverno é frio — winter takes o.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: Está ___ chover. (the European -ing: a)
activities.feedback: Está a chover is the European continuous: está + a + infinitive.

activities.prompt: Read the weather note. What is tomorrow going to be like?
activities.feedback: Amanhã vai estar nublado e vai chover — cloudy and rainy.

activities.body: Telling the time in Portuguese starts with a question you'll use daily: Que horas são? The answer almost always begins with são — São duas, São três — with one famous exception: one o'clock is É uma hora. Minutes attach with a simple e, half past is e meia, and meio-dia and meia-noite handle noon and midnight.

activities.prompt: Which asks the time?
activities.feedback: Que horas são? — literally, what hours are they.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: It's one o'clock. (The famous exception.)
activities.feedback: É uma hora — one o'clock takes é, not são.

activities.prompt: Which is correct?
activities.feedback: É uma hora is the exception that proves the são rule.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: It's half past three.
activities.feedback: São três e meia — e glues the half on.

activities.prompt: Change the time: São três e meia. → It's quarter to four.
activities.feedback: São quatro menos um quarto — menos subtracts.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: ___ meio-dia. (It's)
activities.feedback: É meio-dia — noon takes é like one o'clock.

activities.prompt: Read the station note. When does the train leave?
activities.feedback: O comboio parte às quatro — at four.

activities.body: Dates in Portuguese stack like building blocks: em for in/on, the day number, de, the month — em 3 de maio. Months are lowercase and masculine, and em does double duty for both months (em maio) and full dates (em 3 de maio). Once you can say your birthday — O meu aniversário é em… — the calendar is yours.

activities.prompt: Which month is maio?
activities.feedback: Maio is May — em maio há flores.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: My birthday is in June. (Months are lowercase.)
activities.feedback: O meu aniversário é em junho — junho stays lowercase.

answers: O meu aniversário é em junho.

activities.prompt: Which date is written correctly?
activities.feedback: Em 3 de maio — day, de, lowercase month.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: I arrive on May 3rd.
activities.feedback: Chego em 3 de maio.

activities.prompt: Change the month: Em janeiro faz frio. → In May there are flowers.
activities.feedback: Em maio há flores.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: O ano tem doze ___. (months)
activities.feedback: O ano tem doze meses.

activities.prompt: Read the birthday note. When is the party?
activities.feedback: Em 15 de junho — on June 15th.

activities.body: The market has its own grammar of plenty: name the amount, add de, name the goods. Um quilo de maçãs, uma garrafa de água, uma dúzia de ovos, meio quilo de queijo. De is the little bridge you can't skip. Open with Queria… and you'll be served like a regular; ask É fresco? and you'll be respected like one.

activities.prompt: Which means 'a dozen'?
activities.feedback: Uma dúzia de ovos — a dozen eggs.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: I'd like a kilo of apples. (Amount + de + goods.)
activities.feedback: Queria um quilo de maçãs — don't skip the de.

activities.prompt: Which is correct?
activities.feedback: De bridges amount and goods: um quilo de maçãs.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: A bottle of water, please.
activities.feedback: Uma garrafa de água, por favor.

activities.prompt: Change the amount: Um quilo de maçãs. → Half a kilo of cheese.
activities.feedback: Meio quilo de queijo.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: O peixe é ___? (fresh)
activities.feedback: É fresco? — the market's quality check.

activities.prompt: Which verb goes with futebol?
activities.feedback: Jogar futebol — jogar is for sports with rules.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: I like reading. (Gostar de + infinitive.)
activities.feedback: Gosto de ler — de plus the infinitive.

activities.prompt: Which is correct?
activities.feedback: Gostar always brings de.

activities.prompt: Change the hobby: Gosto de ler. → I like to swim.
activities.feedback: Gosto de nadar — infinitive after de.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: Jogo futebol ___ sábados. (on — aos)
activities.feedback: Aos sábados — on Saturdays.

activities.prompt: Read the weekend note. What does the writer's brother like to do?
activities.feedback: O meu irmão gosta de cozinhar — to cook.

activities.prompt: Which means 'my head hurts'?
activities.feedback: Dói-me a cabeça — the verb doer with -me.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: My arm hurts. (Dói-me + article + part.)
activities.feedback: Dói-me o braço — masculine o for o braço.

activities.prompt: Which is correct?
activities.feedback: The article stays, -me glues after the verb: Dói-me a cabeça.

activities.prompt: Change the symptom: Tenho febre. → I'm sick.
activities.feedback: Estar for states: Estou doente.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: Dói-me ___ cabeça. (the — feminine)
activities.feedback: Dói-me a cabeça — the article is required.

activities.prompt: Read the sick note. When is the writer going to the doctor?
activities.feedback: Amanhã vou ao médico de manhã — tomorrow morning.

activities.body: The farmácia is Portugal's front line of healthcare, and its language is beautifully practical. Preciso de… (I need…) opens every request, para says what it's for — para a dor de cabeça, para a tosse — and de links pain to place: dor de cabeça, dor de costas. Tem receita? is the one question to be ready for.

activities.prompt: Which verb means 'to need'?
activities.feedback: Precisar de — Preciso de aspirina.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: I need aspirin. (Precisar brings de.)
activities.feedback: Preciso de aspirina — never skip the de.

activities.prompt: Which is correct?
activities.feedback: Precisar + de, always.

activities.prompt: Change the need: Preciso de aspirina. → I need a syrup for the cough.
activities.feedback: Preciso de um xarope para a tosse.

answers: Preciso de um xarope para a tosse.

activities.prompt: Read the pharmacy note. What does the pharmacist ask for?
activities.feedback: Tem receita? — do you have a prescription.

activities.body: Nobody wants this lesson, everybody should have it. Socorro! cuts through everything. After that, the imperative takes over: Chame uma ambulância! Chame a polícia! The -e ending keeps it polite even mid-crisis, and É urgente! tells the world to hurry. Onde fica o hospital? is the question to ask before you ever need it.

activities.prompt: Which word cries for help?
activities.feedback: Socorro! — the word that needs no grammar.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: Call an ambulance! (Imperative: Chame…)
activities.feedback: Chame uma ambulância! — the -e ending for strangers.

activities.prompt: Which is the correct emergency command?
activities.feedback: Chame with -e addresses strangers — the safe default.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: Where is the hospital?
activities.feedback: Onde fica o hospital?

activities.prompt: Change who to call: Chame uma ambulância! → Call the police!
activities.feedback: Chame a polícia!

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: É ___! (urgent)
activities.feedback: É urgente! — when seconds matter.

activities.body: Invitations are where Portuguese warmth shows: Queres vir jantar? Gostavas de vir ao cinema? The conditional gostavas turns an ask into a gift. Accept with open arms — Sim, com prazer! Boa ideia! — and decline with a cushion: Desta vez não posso, desculpa. Either way, Obrigado pelo convite keeps the door open.

activities.prompt: Which accepts warmly?
activities.feedback: Sim, com prazer! — yes, with pleasure.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: Do you want to come for dinner? (Queres vir…?)
activities.feedback: Queres vir jantar? — the classic invitation.

activities.prompt: Which declines kindly?
activities.feedback: Desta vez não posso, desculpa — cushioned, not cold.

activities.prompt: Soften the invitation: Queres vir jantar? → Would you like to come to the cinema?
activities.feedback: Gostavas de…? — the conditional softens beautifully.

activities.prompt: Read the invitation. When is the dinner?
activities.feedback: Sábado, às oito — Saturday at eight.

activities.prompt: Which means 'I spoke yesterday'?
activities.feedback: Falei ontem — falei is the pretérito perfeito of falar (-ei ending). Falo is present, falava is the imperfeito, and falar is the infinitive.

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: you (tu) ate, yesterday — '___ o bolo todo?' (Did you eat the whole cake?)
activities.feedback: Comeste o bolo todo? — -er verbs take -este for tu in the perfeito: comeste.

activities.prompt: Which verb is irregular in the pretérito perfeito?
activities.feedback: Fiz — fazer becomes fiz, an irregular. Falei, comi and partiu are all regular formations.

activities.prompt: Say: We bought bread this morning.
activities.feedback: Comprámos pão de manhã — nós form of comprar in the perfeito is comprámos, with the accent.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: Ela ___ às oito. (she left)
activities.feedback: Partiu — ela form of partir in the perfeito: -iu ending.

activities.prompt: Read about yesterday. What did she do in the afternoon?
activities.feedback: She ate a sandwich and left for work at two — 'comi uma sandes e parti para o trabalho às duas'.

answers: She ate a sandwich and left for work.
She ate a sandwich and left for work at two.
Comeu uma sandes e partiu para o trabalho.

activities.body: Now the other past: the world of used-to. Notice the soft -ava and -ia endings in the examples — brincava, comia, estávamos a ver. The imperfeito never tells you something happened once; it tells you how things were. Also note the very Portuguese 'estar a + infinitivo': estávamos a ver = we were watching. Say them out loud and hear the habit in the endings.

activities.prompt: Which describes a habit in the past?
activities.feedback: Brincava na rua — the -ava ending marks the imperfeito: used to play. Brinquei is one completed event, brinco is present.

activities.prompt: Predict the form: he used to eat at seven — 'Ele ___ sempre às sete.'
activities.feedback: Ele comia sempre às sete — -er verbs take -ia in the imperfeito: comia.

activities.prompt: Which verb is irregular in the imperfeito?
activities.feedback: Era — ser becomes era, one of only three irregulars (era, tinha, vinha). Falava, comia and partia are regular.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: When I was a child I used to play in the street.
activities.feedback: Quando era criança, brincava na rua — the quando clause sets the scene, then the habit.

activities.prompt: Say: We were watching TV.
activities.feedback: Estávamos a ver televisão — the very Portuguese past progressive: estar in the imperfeito + a + infinitivo.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: Ele ___ sempre às sete. (he used to eat)
activities.feedback: Comia — imperfeito of comer for ele: -ia ending.

segments.text: sempre às sete. (he used to eat)

activities.prompt: Read about Tiago's childhood. How did he get to school?
activities.feedback: He walked — 'ia a pé para a escola'.

activities.prompt: Which sentence mixes background and event correctly?
activities.feedback: Estava a chover quando cheguei — imperfeito sets the scene (was raining), perfeito is the event (arrived). The other options pair two backgrounds or two events.

options.text: Estava a chover quando estava a chegar.

activities.prompt: Complete the background: 'Enquanto ela ___, ele pôs a mesa.' (she was cooking)
activities.feedback: Enquanto ela cozinhava — enquanto signals ongoing background, so the imperfeito: cozinhava.

answers: Enquanto ela cozinhava, ele pôs a mesa.

activities.prompt: Which word signals a one-time completed event?
activities.feedback: De repente — suddenly marks a single finished event, so it pairs with the perfeito. Todos os dias, sempre and enquanto signal habits or background.

activities.prompt: Say: Suddenly the phone rang.
activities.feedback: De repente, o telemóvel tocou — de repente + perfeito: tocar → tocou.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: ___ a chover quando cheguei. (it was)
activities.feedback: Estava — the background weather takes the imperfeito: estava a chover.

activities.prompt: Which orders the day correctly, morning to night?
activities.feedback: De manhã fui ao mercado, depois almocei, à noite vi um filme — time markers in chronological order with perfeitos. The others scramble the day or mix tenses.

options.text: De manhã fui ao mercado, depois almocei, à noite vi um filme.
À noite fui ao mercado, depois almocei, de manhã vi um filme.
De manhã vou ao mercado, depois almoço, à noite vejo um filme.
De manhã ia ao mercado, depois almoçava, à noite via um filme.

activities.prompt: Predict the sequencer: '___ almocei com os meus pais.' (then)
activities.feedback: Depois almocei com os meus pais — depois links the next event in the chain.

answers: Depois almocei com os meus pais.

activities.prompt: Which word means 'then / afterwards'?
activities.feedback: Depois — then/afterwards. Antes is before, agora is now, já is already.

activities.prompt: Say: It was a great weekend!
activities.feedback: Foi um fim de semana fixe! — foi is the perfeito of ser; fixe is the very Portuguese 'cool/great'.

answers: Foi um fim de semana fixe!
Foi um fim de semana fixe.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: No sábado de manhã ___ ao mercado. (I went)
activities.feedback: Fui — the perfeito of ir for eu. 'No sábado vou' would mean next Saturday.

activities.body: The future you will use every day needs no new verb endings. Look at the examples: vou, vais, vai, vamos, vão — that is just the verb ir, which you know — followed by an infinitivo. Vou fazer, vais sair, vamos viajar. Say them out loud: the plan lives in the little word ir.

activities.prompt: Which says 'I'm going to make dinner'?
activities.feedback: Vou fazer o jantar — vou + infinitivo is the future. Faço is present, fiz is past, and 'vou a fazer' mixes the future with the progressive.

activities.prompt: Predict the form: we are going to travel in August — '___ viajar em agosto.'
activities.feedback: Vamos viajar em agosto — the nós form of ir is vamos, then the infinitivo.

activities.prompt: Which is NOT a future with ir + infinitivo?
activities.feedback: Estou a ir — that is the present progressive (I am going, right now), not a future plan. The other three are all ir + infinitivo.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: Are you going out tonight?
activities.feedback: Vais sair hoje à noite? — vais + infinitivo, time phrase at the end.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: Eles ___ chegar amanhã. (are going to)
activities.feedback: Vão — the eles form of ir: eles vão chegar.

activities.prompt: Which is a promise about the future?
activities.feedback: Serei pontual, prometo — serei is the future of ser. Fui is past, sou is present, era is imperfeito.

activities.prompt: Predict the future: eu falar — 'Amanhã ___ com o chefe.'
activities.feedback: Falarei — infinitivo falar + -ei ending: falarei.

activities.prompt: Falei vs falarei — which one is the future?
activities.feedback: Falarei — the extra syllable and accent mark the future. Falei is the pretérito perfeito (past), falava the imperfeito, falo the present.

activities.prompt: Say: I will help with the suitcases.
activities.feedback: Ajudarei com as malas — ajudar + -ei.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: ___ pontual, prometo. (I will be)
activities.feedback: Serei — the future of ser for eu. Promises love the futuro simples.

activities.prompt: Read João's promises. What will he do in the afternoon?
activities.feedback: He will study for the exam — 'à tarde estudarei para o exame'.

answers: He will study for the exam.

activities.prompt: Which expresses an intention (not a completed change)?
activities.feedback: Tenciono mudar de emprego — tenciono = I intend. Mudei is already done (past), mudo is present habit, mudava is past habit.

activities.prompt: Predict the verb: '___ em viajar para o Brasil.' (I'm thinking of)
activities.feedback: Penso em viajar — pensar em + infinitivo expresses a considered idea.

answers: Penso em viajar para o Brasil.

activities.prompt: Which word means 'to intend'?
activities.feedback: Tencionar — to intend. Tentar is to try, ter is to have, tomar is to take.

activities.prompt: Say: I intend to change jobs this year.
activities.feedback: Tenciono mudar de emprego este ano — tenciono + plain infinitivo.

answers: Tenciono mudar de emprego este ano.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: Vou atualizar o ___ amanhã. (CV)
activities.feedback: Currículo — o currículo, the CV. A concrete first step for any career plan.

activities.body: Would, could, should — the language of gentle hypotheticals. Notice the -ia endings in the examples: falaria, poderia, seria, deverias. Same pattern for every verb: infinitivo + -ia. The most useful one is poder → poderia: it turns any request velvet-soft. Say each example out loud and hear how much kinder poderia sounds than pode.

activities.prompt: Which is the softest, most polite request?
activities.feedback: Poderia ajudar-me? — the condicional (would be able) is the politest form. Podes is direct, ajuda-me is a command, and vou ajudar-te offers help rather than asking.

activities.prompt: Predict the form: '___ ótimo ver-te amanhã.' (it would be great)
activities.feedback: Seria ótimo — the condicional of ser: seria.

activities.prompt: Which verb form means 'would speak'?
activities.feedback: Falaria — infinitivo + -ia = would. Falava is the imperfeito (used to speak), falou is past (spoke), falará is future (will speak).

activities.prompt: Say: It would be great to see you tomorrow.
activities.feedback: Seria ótimo ver-te amanhã — seria + infinitivo.

activities.prompt: Read Rui's request. What does he offer in return?
activities.feedback: Help with the shopping — 'Eu ajudaria com as compras em troca.'

activities.prompt: Which is the softest way to order a coffee?
activities.feedback: Queria um café, por favor — queria (imperfect of querer) is the polite 'would like'. Quero is blunt, dá-me is a command, and a bare 'Um café!' is just pointing with words.

activities.prompt: Predict the form: '___ de reservar uma mesa.' (I would like)
activities.feedback: Gostaria de reservar uma mesa — gostaria de + infinitivo.

activities.prompt: After 'gostaria de', what follows?
activities.feedback: The infinitivo: gostaria de reservar. Never a conjugated verb, never a gerund — de + infinitivo, always.

activities.prompt: Say: We'd like to book a table for two.
activities.feedback: Queríamos reservar uma mesa para dois — the nós form: queríamos.

answers: Queríamos reservar uma mesa para dois.

activities.prompt: Fill the gap: ___ de falar com o gerente. (I would like)
activities.feedback: Gostaria — gostaria de + infinitivo: gostaria de falar.

segments.text: de falar com o gerente. (I would like)
